props.title: Let's Do It Again
props.initialSlug: Double the fun, double the thrill!

sections.content: Let's Do It Again (1975) stands as a pivotal Black comedy that paired Sidney Poitier and Bill Cosby in their second collaboration after Uptown Saturday Night (1974). This hustler comedy showcased Black actors in roles that defied stereotypes, with Poitier directing while starring as Clyde Williams alongside Cosby's Billy Foster. The film follows two working-class friends who hypnotize a boxer to win fights, scamming mobsters through fixed matches. It's part of a significant 1970s wave of Black-directed comedies that included Cotton Comes to Harlem (1970) and Car Wash (1976). Uptown Saturday Night|1974|Sidney Poitier directs this comedy caper about two friends searching for a stolen lottery ticket|Prime Cotton Comes to Harlem|1970|Groundbreaking Black detective comedy following two cops investigating a con man|TCM Car Wash|1976|Ensemble comedy set at an LA car wash featuring Richard Pryor and George Carlin|Netflix

The mid-1970s marked a golden era for Black comedy films that moved beyond the limitations of Blaxploitation. While films like Shaft (1971) dominated the early decade, directors like Poitier crafted more nuanced stories about working-class Black life. Let's Do It Again uses its con-artist plot to explore themes of economic mobility and brotherhood, while maintaining the sharp humor that made these buddy comedies so influential for later films like 48 Hrs. (1982) and Trading Places (1983).

The film's success helped establish a template for Black buddy comedies that would flourish in the 1980s and beyond. The chemistry between Poitier and Cosby influenced later dynamic duos in films like Stir Crazy (1980) and Hollywood Shuffle (1987). The blend of comedy with social commentary about class mobility and hustling to get ahead resonated deeply with audiences and inspired films like Harlem Nights (1989). Stir Crazy|1980|Gene Wilder and Richard Pryor star as wrongly imprisoned friends plotting an escape|HBO Max Hollywood Shuffle|1987|Robert Townsend's satirical look at Black actors' struggles in Hollywood|Criterion Harlem Nights|1989|Eddie Murphy directs and stars in this period comedy about nightclub owners battling gangsters|Prime SUBHEAD: Impact on Black Cinema and Comedy

Poitier's direction in Let's Do It Again demonstrated how Black filmmakers could create mainstream entertainment while maintaining cultural authenticity. The film's success paved the way for directors like Robert Townsend (Hollywood Shuffle), Spike Lee (Do the Right Thing (1989)), and Keenen Ivory Wayans (I'm Gonna Git You Sucka (1988)) to pursue their unique visions in the following decades.
